doc.title: Ray Bryant interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Accompanying singers versus horn players
summary: His approach is the same: support and embellish; keys are rarely a problem.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Interesting. Sonny Rollins you’ve played with, Betty Carter. Is it different playing behind singers than horn players?

Well I always approach it the same way, the same way. I would say to me it’s not too much of a difference because I feel like whether I’m playing for a horn player or for a singer, my role is to support, and wherever I can embellish. So I do the same thing for a horn player that I would do for a singer in regards to that. So I don’t see too much difference in playing. I mean some guys do it differently, but my approach would be the same for a singer as for a horn player. If a horn player is playing a ballad, I do the same thing I would do basically if a singer were singing this same ballad. So I approach them similarly.
Is it a problem sometimes, or a challenge, when you have to play perhaps the same tune but if you’re playing it with a vocalist, a tune you’ve played many times, all of a sudden it’s in a new key?
Oh this can be a problem, but it shouldn’t be — I guess I’m fortunate it’s never been a big problem for me. Most anything I can play I can play in almost any key. It doesn’t make any difference.
